bottom_line: In patients stabilised after an acute coronary syndrome, rivaroxaban versus placebo increased clinically significant bleeding in a dose-dependent manner (hazard ratios [HRs] 2.21 [95% CI 1.25–3.91] for 5 mg, 3.35 [2.31–4.87] for 10 mg, 3.60 [2.32–5.58] for 15 mg, and 5.06 [3.45–7.42] for 20 mg doses; p<0.0001).
implications: These phase II data show that, compared with placebo, rivaroxaban increased clinically significant bleeding in a graded, dose-dependent manner (HRs 2.21 to 5.06 across 5–20 mg total daily doses; p<0.0001). The primary efficacy composite was not statistically different (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.60–1.05; p=0.10), while the main secondary composite (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke) was lower with rivaroxaban (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.96; p=0.0270); the results support a possible reduction in major ischaemic outcomes but do not establish definitive benefit on the primary efficacy endpoint.

major_points.text: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II dose-escalation trial in 3491 post-ACS patients across 297 sites in 27 countries.
major_points.quote: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II, dose-escalation study, 3491 participants were randomised at 297 sites in 27 countries.

major_points.text: Patients were randomised 1:1:1 within strata and dose tier to placebo, rivaroxaban once daily, or the same total daily dose twice daily.
major_points.quote: Participants were randomised within each strata and dose tier with a block randomisation method at 1:1:1 to receive either placebo or rivaroxaban (at doses 5–20 mg) given once daily or the same total daily dose given twice daily.

major_points.text: Primary safety endpoint was clinically significant bleeding (TIMI major, TIMI minor, or requiring medical attention).
major_points.quote: The primary safety endpoint was clinically signiﬁcant bleeding (TIMI major, TIMI minor, or requiring medical attention)

major_points.text: Primary efficacy endpoint (death, MI, stroke, or severe recurrent ischaemia requiring revascularisation) was 5.6% with rivaroxaban vs 7.0% with placebo (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.60–1.05; p=0.10).

major_points.text: Main secondary efficacy endpoint (death, MI, or stroke) was reduced with rivaroxaban vs placebo (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.96; p=0.0270).
major_points.quote: Rivaroxaban reduced the main secondary eﬃcacy endpoint of death, myocardial infarction, or stroke compared with placebo (87/2331 [3·9%] vs 62/1160 [5·5%]; HR 0·69, [95% CI 0·50–0·96], p=0·0270).

major_points.text: Clinically significant bleeding increased in a dose-dependent manner versus placebo.
major_points.quote: The risk of clinically signiﬁcant bleeding with rivaroxaban versus placebo increased in a dose-dependent manner (hazard ratios [HRs] 2·21 [95% CI 1·25–3·91] for 5 mg, 3·35 [2·31–4·87] for 10 mg, 3·60 [2·32–5·58] for 15 mg, and 5·06 [3·45–7·42] for 20 mg doses; p<0·0001).

major_points.text: One fatal bleed occurred (intracranial haemorrhage) in the rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily group of stratum 1.
major_points.quote: One fatal bleed occurred: a participant in the rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily dose group of stratum 1 presented with an intracranial haemorrhage.

criticisms.text: Many dosing permutations meant some individual dosing strategies had small numbers of patients, making it unclear whether observations were due to chance or biology.
